title: After the Bag Is Empty: Delayed Hemolysis, Lookback and Window Periods
summary: Recognize a delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction from an evanescent antibody, know why early tests can be negative, and follow a donor lookback with HBV window periods and Babesia screening in mind.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 41 Hit 9 (anamnestic DHTR), Hit 14 (HBV windows), Hit 23 (lookback), Hit 25 (transfusion-transmitted Babesia) and Trap 6. Checked against Furqan 2026, Glover & Maitta 2026, Vellanki 2025, 21 CFR 610.46, Badawi 2025, Bloch 2026 and CDC DPDx. Hit 14 says HBV NAT catches the core window; Badawi 2025 shows anti-HBc may be the only marker there, while NAT shortens the early window (register flag rv-hbv-core-window). US lookback rules only; Philippine rules not checked. Not taught: the 1–6-week Babesia timing, per-unit infection-risk figures (Hit 13) and ISBT 128 (Hit 15) — sources not read.

objectives: Explain how an evanescent alloantibody causes a delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction.
Recognize DHTR laboratory findings and why early DAT and antibody screens can be negative.
Outline the steps of a US HIV lookback after a reactive donor test.
Distinguish the HBV early window (NAT) from the core window (anti-HBc) and recognize transfusion-transmitted Babesia.

scenes.title: Two trails that start after the bag is empty
scenes.altText: Left: a recipient card — transfused 2 red-cell units on day 0 with a negative antibody screen; on day 7 hemoglobin is lower than before the transfusion and the patient is jaundiced. Right: a donor card — a regular donor’s new donation is HIV NAT reactive; earlier donations went to other hospitals. Two arrows point back in time: “back to the recipient’s antibodies” and “back to the donor’s earlier units”.

cues.text: A patient received two red-cell units with a negative antibody screen. A week later, the hemoglobin is lower than before the transfusion, and the patient is jaundiced.
Meanwhile, a regular blood donor’s newest donation tests reactive for HIV. Earlier donations from that donor have already been shipped.
Both problems start after the bag is empty. The lab must follow two trails back in time.

scenes.title: The antibody that hid
scenes.altText: A timeline with an antibody-level line. Years ago: pregnancy or transfusion → an alloantibody (for example anti-Jkᵃ) rises, then falls below the detection line of the antibody screen (“evanescent”). Day 0: the screen is negative, antigen-positive red cells are transfused. Days 3–21: anamnestic (memory) response — the antibody shoots back up and coats the transfused cells, which are cleared. A list token: usual systems — Rh, Kidd, Duffy, Kell, MNS.

cues.text: Years ago, a pregnancy or transfusion made this patient form an alloantibody, for example anti-Jk-a.
Over time the antibody fell below the level an antibody screen can detect. It did not vanish; it was hiding. These are called evanescent antibodies.
On day 0 the screen was negative, so antigen-positive cells were given. That re-exposure triggered a memory response.
Between about 3 and 21 days later, the antibody shot back up and coated the transfused cells, which were destroyed. That is a delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction.
The antibodies usually belong to the Rh, Kidd, Duffy, Kell or MNS systems, not ABO.

props.label: Usual systems: Rh · Kidd · Duffy · Kell · MNS

scenes.title: What the lab sees — and when it sees it
scenes.altText: A results card fills in for day 7: hemoglobin below pre-transfusion level, LDH high, bilirubin up, haptoglobin undetectable; DAT positive for IgG; new antibody identified (anti-Jkᵃ). A caution card: early in a DHTR, the antibody screen and DAT may still be negative despite hemolysis; positives can lag several days behind the hemoglobin nadir — repeat testing. A records card: check the patient’s transfusion-service history; missing records hide earlier antibodies.

cues.text: By day 7, the lab sees hemolysis: hemoglobin below the pre-transfusion value, high LDH and bilirubin, and an undetectable haptoglobin.
The direct antiglobulin test is positive for IgG, and the antibody screen now finds a new antibody, here anti-Jk-a.
But timing matters. Early in a delayed reaction, the screen and the DAT can still be negative despite brisk hemolysis.
Positives may lag several days behind the lowest hemoglobin. So a negative DAT does not rule out a delayed reaction; repeat the tests.
And check the records. An antibody found at another time or another hospital may now be below detection. Missing records hide it.

Check antibody records
lines: Past antibody may be undetectable now

scenes.title: The donor trail: lookback, and why windows matter
scenes.altText: A lookback card (US, 21 CFR 610.46, HIV): within 3 calendar days of a reactive donor test, the collecting establishment reviews records for earlier donations (those collected within 12 months before the donor’s last nonreactive screening test); quarantines in-date units and notifies consignees; performs further testing; reports results to consignees within 45 days. The transfusion service then notifies recipients or their physicians, making reasonable attempts within 12 weeks. Lookback is not a recall. A window card for HBV: NAT detects HBV DNA first (on average 6–15 days before HBsAg) — the early window; after HBsAg clears and before anti-HBs appears, anti-HBc may be the only positive marker — the core window. A Babesia card: RBC-containing products transmit B. microti; FDA-approved NAT screening in endemic states since 2019; tetrads on a Giemsa smear.

cues.text: Now the donor trail. In the US, within 3 calendar days of a reactive HIV test, the blood center reviews records to find the donor’s earlier donations.
In-date units from those earlier donations are quarantined, the hospitals that received them are notified, and further testing results follow within 45 days.
If confirmed, the transfusion service notifies earlier recipients or their physicians, within 12 weeks. This is a lookback, not a recall.
Why do earlier donations matter? Windows. For hepatitis B, NAT finds viral DNA days to weeks before HBsAg: the early window. In the later core window, anti-HBc may be the only positive marker.
Babesia, a red-cell parasite, travels in any red-cell product. Donors in endemic US states are screened by NAT. On a smear, look for tetrads.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards appear in turn: “A negative DAT rules out a delayed hemolytic reaction” (✓ early on, DAT and screen can be negative — repeat); “HBV NAT closes the core window” (✓ NAT shortens the early window; anti-HBc covers the core window); “Lookback is a product recall” (✓ federal rules say lookback actions are not a recall).

cues.text: Trap one: a negative DAT rules out a delayed hemolytic reaction. No. Early on, the DAT and the screen can still be negative. Repeat them.
Trap two: HBV NAT closes the core window. No. NAT shortens the early window before HBsAg; in the core window, anti-HBc may be the only marker.
Trap three: a lookback is a recall. No. US rules state that lookback actions are not a recall.

scenes.title: Hidden antibody, hidden virus — look back both ways
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Hidden antibody, hidden virus — look back both ways.” Two tokens: recipient side — evanescent antibody returns in 3–21 days, check records, repeat DAT; donor side — window periods, lookback quarantine and notify. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: hidden antibody, hidden virus, look back both ways. On the recipient side, a hidden antibody returns within weeks. On the donor side, a hidden infection is found later, and earlier units are traced.
Where it breaks: some delayed reactions are serologic only, without hemolysis; lookback rules differ by country and by infection; and window lengths depend on the assay and pooling.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “DHTR: evanescent antibody returns in 3–21 days · DAT/screen may lag · check records”, “Lookback: quarantine and notify (not a recall) · HBV NAT = early window, anti-HBc = core window”.

cues.text: A delayed hemolytic reaction comes from a hidden antibody that returns days to weeks later, so repeat negative tests and check records; a reactive donor triggers a lookback of earlier units because infections hide in window periods.

props.label: DHTR: hidden antibody returns in 3–21 d · DAT/screen may lag · check records
Lookback: quarantine + notify (not a recall) · HBV NAT = early window · anti-HBc = core window

explanation.what: Plain language: some reactions happen days after a transfusion because an old antibody, too weak to detect, wakes up; and some infections are found in a donor only later, so earlier blood from that donor is traced. Scientific terms: delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction (DHTR), anamnestic response, evanescent antibody, DAT, lookback, consignee, window period, HBV NAT, anti-HBc, Babesia microti.
explanation.why: Alloantibodies from pregnancy or transfusion can fall below detection thresholds and rise rapidly on re-exposure. Window periods exist because each marker appears at a different time after infection: HBV DNA first, then HBsAg; after HBsAg clears, anti-HBc may be the only marker before anti-HBs.
explanation.measure: DHTR typically 3–21 days after RBC transfusion; Hb falls, LDH and bilirubin rise, haptoglobin falls; DAT IgG positive with a new non-ABO antibody — but screens and DAT may be negative early. US HIV lookback (21 CFR 610.46): record review within 3 calendar days; quarantine in-date units collected ≤ 12 months before the last nonreactive screen; notify consignees; further testing; consignee notification of results within 45 days; recipient notification attempts within 12 weeks. HBV NAT detects DNA on average 6–15 days before HBsAg.
explanation.differs: Delayed hemolytic reactions (non-ABO antibodies, days to weeks) vs reactions at the time of transfusion; lookback vs recall; early window vs core window.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: DHTR timing and mechanism, negative DAT not excluding DHTR, lookback steps, which marker covers which HBV window, and Babesia on a post-transfusion smear.

questions.stem: Ten days after a red-cell transfusion, a patient’s hemoglobin falls below the pre-transfusion value, with high LDH and undetectable haptoglobin. The pre-transfusion antibody screen was negative. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: An anamnestic rise of a previously formed, undetectable alloantibody
options.rationale: Correct. Evanescent antibodies can fall below detection and return within about 3–21 days after re-exposure.
Incorrect. Delayed reactions are caused by non-ABO alloantibodies; nothing here points to an ABO error.
Incorrect. That causes fever, not delayed hemolysis.

options.text: A negative screen proves no antibody is involved
options.rationale: Incorrect. A negative screen can miss an antibody below the detection threshold.

questions.stem: A donor’s new donation is confirmed HIV positive. Under 21 CFR 610.46, what must the hospital transfusion service (consignee) do with in-date units from that donor’s earlier donations?

options.text: Quarantine them when notified, and notify earlier recipients or their physicians if further testing is positive
options.rationale: Correct. Consignees quarantine on notification and make reasonable attempts to notify recipients within 12 weeks.

options.text: Keep issuing them; earlier donations tested negative
options.rationale: Incorrect. Earlier donations may have been collected in a window period.

options.text: Treat it as a product recall and wait for the FDA
options.rationale: Incorrect. Lookback actions are not a recall under the regulation.
Incorrect. Release, destruction or relabelling follows the further-testing results and is documented.

questions.stem: A donor is HBsAg negative and anti-HBs negative but anti-HBc positive. Which phase of HBV infection is most likely, and which marker reveals it?

options.text: Core window — anti-HBc may be the only positive marker
options.rationale: Correct. After HBsAg clears and before anti-HBs appears, anti-HBc may be the only marker.

options.text: Early window — detected only by NAT
options.rationale: Incorrect. The early window comes before HBsAg and before anti-HBc; NAT detects DNA first.
Incorrect. Vaccination gives anti-HBs without anti-HBc.
Incorrect. Chronic infection is HBsAg positive.

references.citation: Furqan M, Rana MA, Iloke CV, et al. Anti-Jka-mediated delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction mimicking warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia in a multiparous woman: a case report. Ann Med Surg (Lond). 2026;88(6):3729-3733.
references.usedFor: DHTR typically 3–21 days after RBC transfusion; recipient alloantibodies against non-ABO antigens (Rh, Kidd, Duffy, Kell, MNS); usually anamnestic after prior transfusion or pregnancy; hemolysis labs (LDH, bilirubin, undetectable haptoglobin), DAT IgG positive, anti-Jka; missing antibody records limited assessment.

references.citation: Glover RT, Maitta RW. Antibody-dependent and antibody-independent hemolysis in sickle cell disease. Antibodies (Basel). 2026;15(4):70.
references.usedFor: Evanescent antibodies are present below detection thresholds and increase rapidly on re-exposure; DHTR symptoms days to weeks after transfusion; DAT may be falsely negative with severe intravascular hemolysis.

references.citation: Vellanki S, Thalambedu N, Kumar AKTA, et al. Navigating hyperhemolysis in sickle cell disease: insights from literature. Diagnostics (Basel). 2025;15(14):1835.
references.usedFor: During a DHTR, initial antibody screens and DATs may be negative despite significant hemolysis; about four days from the lowest hemoglobin to the first positive DAT or screen.

references.citation: 21 CFR 610.46, Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) “lookback” requirements (eCFR, version 2026-01-01, accessed 2026-10-08).
references.usedFor: Collecting establishment: within 3 calendar days review records for donations collected ≤ 12 months before the last nonreactive screen (or reactive NAT with nonreactive antibody); quarantine in-date units and notify consignees; further testing; notify consignees of results within 45 days; release/destroy/relabel. Consignee: quarantine when notified; notify recipients or physician of record, reasonable attempts within 12 weeks. (c) Not a recall.

references.citation: Badawi MA, Eldakhakhny S, Ali M, et al. Key challenges in screening blood donors for hepatitis B virus. Viruses. 2025;18(1):23.
references.usedFor: NAT has the shortest window (10–20 days after infection); HBV DNA detected up to 40 days (mean 6–15 days) before HBsAg; after HBsAg resolution and before anti-HBs, anti-HBc may be the only positive marker; residual risk from window-period donations and occult HBV.

references.citation: Bloch EM, Jacobs JW, Vannier E, et al. Guidance on the management of asymptomatic blood donors who test positive for Babesia. Clin Infect Dis. 2026;83(1):e206-e213.
references.usedFor: B. microti predominant in North America, endemic in the Northeast and upper Midwest; transmissible via any RBC-containing product; TTB mortality up to 19%; since 2019 FDA-approved NAT donor screening in 14 states and DC; TTB now rare.

references.citation: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, DPDx. Babesiosis.
references.usedFor: Tetrads in Giemsa-stained thin blood smears are a dividing form characteristic of Babesia.
